score_rationale: Moderate-to-strong willingness-to-pay validated by active commercial market: at least 5 vendors (Power Almanac, InfoGlobalData, ContactOut, ITNow Technologies, AverickMedia) currently selling municipal government official contact databases with Power Almanac offering 250,000 records across 21,000+ cities, counties, and townships organized by verified roles. Four high-value B2B buyer segments: (1) government technology (GovTech) vendors (Tyler Technologies, CivicPlus, Granicus, OpenGov, Cartegraph) selling municipal software for permitting, licensing, tax collection, asset management, public works, recreation management, and citizen engagement portals at $10,000-$500,000/year per municipality depending on population and module coverage — GovTech vendors pay $8,000-$20,000/year for targeted municipal official marketing lists to acquire customers with $50,000-$500,000/year contract values; (2) infrastructure and public works contractors (civil engineering firms, road paving contractors, water/wastewater treatment system vendors, traffic signal and streetlight providers, fleet management and municipal vehicle vendors) bidding on capital improvement projects ranging $500,000-$50M+ for road reconstruction, water main replacement, wastewater plant upgrades, and municipal building construction — one signed contract justifies significant prospecting investment; (3) municipal bond underwriters and public finance advisors (Raymond James, Stifel, PFM Financial Advisors, Baker Tilly Municipal Advisors) providing debt issuance, bond structuring, and financial planning services to cities and counties — municipal bond deals range $5M-$500M+ with underwriter fees of 0.5-2.0% ($25,000-$10M per transaction); and (4) government consulting firms, grant writing services, economic development consultants, and municipal training providers selling services at $50,000-$300,000/year per engagement. Municipal government directories are public record: many cities and counties publish staff directories on official websites with names, titles, departments, email addresses, and phone numbers for elected officials (mayors, city council members, county commissioners) and appointed department heads (city managers, finance directors, public works directors, police chiefs, fire chiefs, planning directors). State municipal leagues (League of California Cities, Texas Municipal League, etc.) maintain member directories. However, no centralized federal database exists — data must be aggregated from 21,000+ individual municipal websites, state municipal league directories, and regional council of governments (COG) listings. Zero PII — all public official contact data under state open records laws and municipal transparency requirements. Engineering lift is moderate-to-high: web scraping or manual extraction from 21,000+ city/county websites, normalization of job titles and departments across municipalities (e.g., 'City Manager' vs. 'City Administrator' vs. 'Town Manager'), deduplication, ongoing maintenance as officials change positions. No affordable flat-file competitor exists on Gumroad or similar marketplaces — Power Almanac likely sells via subscription; no one-time CSV competitor identified. Audience size is substantial: 21,000+ cities, counties, and townships with 250,000+ elected officials and department heads (average ~12 key decision-makers per municipality), creating a TAM of 3,000+ potential B2B buyers across GovTech, infrastructure contractors, municipal finance, and consulting verticals. Score is 7 due to validated moderate-to-strong willingness-to-pay from GovTech and infrastructure sectors with high contract values ($10K-$50M range), confirmed public data availability via municipal websites and state leagues, absence of low-cost flat-file alternatives, substantial official count (250K+ across 21K municipalities), and four distinct B2B buyer segments with proven high-value purchasing behavior in government services market. Score is held at 7 (not elevated to 8) due to moderate-to-high engineering complexity for 21,000-municipality aggregation with no centralized federal database and high data maintenance burden as officials change positions (turnover after elections, retirements, appointments).

data_wanted: Municipal government staff directories are public record under state open records laws and municipal transparency requirements. Cities, counties, and townships (all 21,000+ general-purpose local governments in the US) publish official directories on municipal websites listing elected officials and key department heads. State municipal leagues (League of California Cities, Texas Municipal League, Florida League of Cities, etc. across all 50 states) maintain member directories with mayor and city manager contact information. Regional councils of governments (COGs) and metropolitan planning organizations (MPOs) also publish member jurisdiction rosters. No centralized federal database exists — data must be aggregated from 21,000+ sources. Key fields per official record: municipality name, official full name (first, middle initial, last), title or position (mayor, vice mayor, city council member, county commissioner, township trustee, city manager, town administrator, county administrator, chief administrative officer CAO, finance director, treasurer, controller, public works director, city engineer, police chief, fire chief, planning & zoning director, community development director, parks & recreation director, economic development director, IT director/CIO, human resources director, purchasing agent, city clerk, city attorney), department (executive, finance, public works, police, fire, planning, parks, IT, HR, etc.), office mailing address (street, city, state, ZIP), direct phone number, email address (where publicly listed — some municipalities publish all emails, others list only general department emails), municipality population (from US Census), county, state, form of government (mayor-council, council-manager, commission, town meeting), and municipal website URL. Target elected officials (mayors, city council, county commissioners) and key appointed department heads only — exclude lower-level staff (administrative assistants, clerks, line workers). Scope to general-purpose local governments (cities, counties, townships) — exclude special districts (water districts, fire districts, school districts, which are covered separately). Approximately 21,000 municipalities with ~250,000 elected officials and department heads nationwide (average ~12 key decision-makers per municipality: 1 mayor, 5-7 council members, 5-6 department directors). Target output: 250K rows, one per official. Data is 100% public per state open records acts (e.g., CA Public Records Act, TX Public Information Act, FL Sunshine Law) and municipal charter transparency requirements mandating public access to elected official and department head contact information.

(1) GovTech vendors: municipal software contracts generate $10,000-$500,000/year in recurring revenue across multi-year agreements; vendors routinely pay $8,000-$20,000/year for municipal official marketing lists (implied by Power Almanac's premier positioning and InfoGlobalData commercial presence), making a $149 one-time CSV deliver 53×-134× cost savings. A single acquired municipality customer yields 67×-3,356× ROI vs. database cost. (2) Infrastructure contractors: capital improvement project contracts of $500,000-$50M+ for road reconstruction, water/wastewater upgrades, and facility construction make a $149 prospect database trivial — one signed project yields 3,356×-335,570× ROI. Public works contractors routinely spend $10,000-$50,000/year on business development, bid preparation, and prospect research, making a $149 comprehensive municipal directory a no-brainer. (3) Municipal bond underwriters: bond deals of $5M-$500M+ generate underwriter fees of 0.5-2.0% ($25,000-$10M per transaction) — a single closed deal yields 167×-67,114× ROI vs. $149 database. Public finance advisors serve municipalities for decades across multiple bond issuances, creating cumulative client LTV of $500K-$10M+. (4) Government consultants and grant writers: $50,000-$300,000/year per engagement makes a $149 database negligible — one retained municipality yields 335×-2,013× ROI. However, engineering complexity is moderate-to-high (21,000-source aggregation with no centralized database) and data maintenance burden is substantial (officials change positions after elections, retirements, appointments — estimated 15-25% annual turnover in elected positions and 10-15% in appointed positions). The absence of any flat-file competitor below $1,000 (Power Almanac likely subscription-based, no CSV alternative identified) creates a gap, but harvest and maintenance costs may reduce margins vs. other opportunities with centralized public databases.
